answers:
1. It was the existing SCADA pressure sensors, and we bought no new hardware. The best leak story is the one Carlos Ruiz, one of our field techs, traced using the model's alerts: a major main leak under an elementary school. I don't have the exact location or what the pressure signature looked like to hand, so I'd skip those details.

2. I don't really know what people did with that data before, so I'd rather not guess. The point is that the sensors were already there and we got more out of them without adding anything.

3. It took 18 months to go from 14% to 9%, and the project saves about 410 million gallons a year. I don't have a leak count or miles of main, and I can't say whether all of the drop came from this work, so I'd leave that claim soft.

4. First, about 30% of the alerts were false positives in the first months, so expect that early on. Second, I don't think the machine learning was essential. I believe simple threshold rules got most of the gains. Third, it cost only $85,000 total, which is a good thing to tell other utilities. I don't have a "what I'd do differently" answer for you.

5. I'm Dr. Naomi Fischer, Senior Water Systems Engineer at Mesa Valley Water Authority. I've been there 12 years, and I have a PhD from Arizona State. I'm not sure how to describe my exact role on the project, and I haven't decided on the audience, so I'd skip that for now.

<final>
Finding Leaks with Pressure Data We Already Had

Abstract

Mesa Valley Water Authority found leaks using the SCADA pressure sensors it already had. We bought no new hardware. Over 18 months, non-revenue water went from 14% to 9%, and the project saves about 410 million gallons a year. Total cost was $85,000.

Carlos Ruiz, one of our field techs, used the model's alerts to trace a major main leak under an elementary school. The alerts weren't clean, though. About 30% were false positives in the first months, and other utilities should expect that early on. I also don't think the machine learning was essential. I believe simple threshold rules got most of the gains.

Short Bio

Dr. Naomi Fischer is a Senior Water Systems Engineer at Mesa Valley Water Authority, where she has worked for 12 years. She has a PhD from Arizona State.
</final>
